item.title: Ozone hole one of the largest in decades
item.description:
Waypoint is curating and commenting on third-party reporting. Original publisher: Phys.org.
Summary: In contrast to the 2025 seasonal ozone hole above Antarctica, which was the fifth smallest since 1992, this year's ozone hole ranks as one of the largest in 48 years, based on long-term atmospheric observations, including data from the Copernicus Sentinel-5P satellite. While this may sound alarming, it is important to remember that the size of the ozone hole varies naturally from year to year, and the long-term recovery of the ozone layer remains on track.
Waypoint’s Take: An outdoor reader can treat this as field context — let phenology guide attention outdoors without forcing a schedule on the land. Keep the publisher’s claims provisional until you read the original. Dashboard conditions can sit beside this report before you leave.

item.description:

Summary: Each spring, warmer temperatures can bring earlier leaf-out, while rising atmospheric carbon dioxide can stimulate plant growth, allowing land ecosystems to absorb more carbon. Yet a study published in Nature Plants on Nov. 27 finds that this climate-driven greening has an overlooked brake: fine particulate air pollution, or PM2.5.
